parsed.explanation: The division is comparatively protective — no state bathroom ban, no sex-defining law, governor vetoes of youth-care and sports bans, a state nondiscrimination executive order, and a low-risk assessment — but the national regime governs the unavoidable border and federal stages. Entry screening can refuse or tag X/mismatched documents, with fraud/lifetime-ineligibility risk and reports of confiscated passports and stranded travelers. Federal facilities exclude by birth sex, and immigration/federal custody has documented severe abuse. State-level everyday exposure is lower, but no statewide gender-identity nondiscrimination or hate-crime coverage leaves patchy recourse. Court challenges make some rules uncertain, but current operative exposure is real.

entry_documents.exposure: National binary sex-marker policy; X not processed; discrepancy or reasonable doubt can trigger refusal, case-note tag, and fraud/lifetime ineligibility; reports of confiscated or blocked passports and stranded travelers.
entry_documents.protection: Existing X passports remain valid until expiry; litigation and a legal-aid FAQ exist, but no documented border protocol protects trans visitors.
entry_documents.interaction: The visitor's home passport meets national visa and border screening; a discrepancy can escalate to secondary inspection or refusal before state protections apply.

investigation_detention_custody.exposure: Immigration custody reports forced labour, beatings, solitary confinement and severe sexual abuse; federal corrections policies include conversion practices; detention can follow document discrepancy.
investigation_detention_custody.protection: No documented visitor-specific safeguard; consular access for detained trans travelers is not documented.
investigation_detention_custody.interaction: A border document issue can move the traveler into national immigration custody, bypassing state-level protections.

federal_state_facilities.exposure: National executive order bars transgender people from government-funded single-sex facilities congruent with identity, creating exposure in federal buildings and airports.
federal_state_facilities.protection: The division has no bathroom or facility ban and no law defining sex to exclude transgender people; state executive order and local ordinances protect some services.
federal_state_facilities.interaction: State facilities are relatively safe, but federal facilities follow the national exclusion.

care_services.exposure: National funding pressure caused two hospital systems to pause youth pharmacologic care; national rules threaten insurance coverage for under-18 care. Adult visitor refill access is not documented.
care_services.protection: No state ban; governor vetoed a youth-care ban; the state attorney general joined a challenge to the national declaration; state insurance protections exist for residents.
care_services.interaction: Visitor emergency or refill care may face national funding and policy friction; state law does not ban care but cannot fully shield from national payment rules.

threat_framing_law_enforcement.exposure: National counterterrorism strategy names 'radically pro-transgender' groups; a national justice department memo references 'radical gender ideology'; executive orders target school support for trans minors.
threat_framing_law_enforcement.protection: The division is rated low-risk; a state executive order bars discrimination in state employment and services; a city police department stopped listing crime victims' gender.
threat_framing_law_enforcement.interaction: National rhetoric raises risk if the traveler is perceived as an activist; state institutions are less hostile.

minors_guardians.exposure: National executive order frames youth gender-affirming care as mutilation and directs investigation or prosecution of teachers using preferred names or pronouns; national insurance rules target under-18 care; hospital pauses occurred.
minors_guardians.protection: The division has no youth-care ban; the governor vetoed one; the state attorney general challenges the national declaration.
minors_guardians.interaction: A trans minor travelling with a guardian faces border document scrutiny and possible national care-payment barriers; state law is protective but not a shield from federal action.

street_violence_police_response.exposure: No state gender-identity hate-crime protection; local ordinances cover only about 21 per cent of the population fully and 12 per cent partially; no documented trans-specific violence pattern in the division.
street_violence_police_response.protection: Low-risk assessment; state executive order; some local ordinances; police gender-listing change; national gender-identity hate-crime statute.
street_violence_police_response.interaction: State recourse is patchy; national hate-crime law exists but local enforcement varies.

remedies_unknowns.exposure: No statewide gender-identity nondiscrimination law; no state gender-identity hate-crime coverage; local protections are patchwork; national court challenges remain unresolved.
remedies_unknowns.protection: State executive order, local ordinances, governor vetoes, state attorney general challenge, legal-aid FAQ, and national hate-crime statute.
remedies_unknowns.interaction: A visitor may find local recourse in some cities but no statewide remedy; national measures may be enjoined or change.

anchor_checks.comparison: Similar administrative denial with no jail outcome, but this dossier adds documented national immigration-custody abuse and fraud/lifetime-ineligibility risk, while the division's no-bathroom-ban and low-risk posture are mitigations. Net slightly above that anchor.

That anchor has an ombudsman securing release and no detention; ours lacks a documented border remedy and carries federal custody and facility exposure, so it is materially lower despite the division's protective state posture.

That anchor has strong anti-discrimination enforcement and only clerical billing uncertainty; ours has universal border and document screening, federal facility exclusion, and severe custody risk, so it is far lower.

parsed.synthesis: The division is one of the less hostile state/province environments, but the combined regime is dominated by national border and federal custody/facility rules. A trans visitor with an X or mismatched passport faces the sharpest exposure before entering; once past the border, state facilities and most private venues are not under a bathroom ban, and state employment and services have some protection. Recourse is patchwork, and national detention and custody are severe. The rating sits at the low end of Elevated Risk: state-level mitigation is real but cannot neutralize the unavoidable national entry and federal exposure.
